failures.title: Mercedes-Benz OM611 Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: Swirl Flap Actuator Failure - All variants, especially .940 and .950
items.whatHappens: The plastic gears inside the electronic swirl flap motor strip over time, causing the ECU to throw a check engine light and default the engine to limp mode. In some cases, the flaps themselves can seize in the inlet manifold.
items.repairVsReplace: The actuator motor can be replaced independently and relatively cheaply. However, if the flaps are seized or the manifold is heavily carboned, a full inlet manifold replacement is required.

items.title: Injector Seal Weeping ("Black Death") - All variants
items.whatHappens: The copper washer seals at the base of the injectors degrade, allowing high-pressure combustion gases to escape. This creates a black, crusty carbon buildup around the injector heads, leading to a distinct tapping noise, rough idling, and a strong smell of exhaust in the cabin.
items.repairVsReplace: This is a routine maintenance item, not a terminal failure. Replacing the seals and cleaning the cylinder head is inexpensive and should be done preventatively.

items.title: Timing Chain and Guide Wear - High-mileage units
items.whatHappens: While more robust than later N47 designs, the OM611 timing chain and plastic guide rails can still stretch and wear at very high mileages, leading to a rattling noise on cold starts.
items.repairVsReplace: If caught early, a timing chain and guide kit replacement is straightforward. If ignored, it can jump a tooth, causing valve-to-piston contact and requiring a full engine replacement.

failures.goodYearsLine: The OM611 is widely regarded as a significant reliability step up from the OM604 pre-chamber engine it replaced. Units maintained with regular oil changes and timely injector seal replacements routinely exceed 250,000 miles without major internal issues .

variants.title: OM611 Sub-Codes Explained - Which One Is in Your Car?
variants.intro: ═══════════════════════════════════════ INTRO: The OM611 family shares the same fundamental common-rail block and head design, but displacement, turbocharging, and calibration vary depending on the chassis. Identifying your exact sub-code ensures you order the correct injection pump, turbo, and ancillary components. - Fitted to: C-Class W203 (C 200 CDI), E-Class W210 (E 200 CDI) - Key technical difference: The entry-level variant, featuring a smaller 2151cc displacement and a simpler, lower-boost turbocharger setup (or naturally aspirated in very early W210 applications). - Sub-code-specific failure note: Shares the family failure pattern above; swirl flap actuator failure is highly prevalent on this specific tune. - Interchange note: Not a straight swap with the .960 turbo variants; the injection pump, ECU mapping, and turbo plumbing differ significantly. - Fitted to: E-Class W211 (E 220 CDI), CLK-Class W209 (CLK 220 CDI) - Key technical difference: Increased displacement to 2148cc for better mid-range torque, making it the preferred choice for the heavier W211 E-Class chassis. - Sub-code-specific failure note: Shares the family failure pattern above. - Interchange note: Requires matching injection pump and ECU; the sump, oil pickup, and engine mounts differ between the W211 and W209 applications. - Fitted to: E-Class W211 (E 220 CDI high-output), Sprinter 903/904/906 (213 CDI, 216 CDI) - Key technical difference: Higher boost pressure, upgraded intercooler, and commercial-grade ancillary brackets designed for the heavier load demands of the Sprinter van range. - Sub-code-specific failure note: Shares the family failure pattern above; turbocharger actuator wear and EGR clogging are more prevalent on this variant due to higher boost loads and commercial duty cycles. - Interchange note: Passenger car and Sprinter versions share the core block architecture, but the oil pickup, sump, and accessory drives are application-specific and not directly interchangeable without significant modification.

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement OM611 Engine - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: A used OM611 engine makes sense only if it comes with verifiable service history and documented replacement of the swirl flap actuator and injector seals. Given the age of these vehicles, the primary risk is hidden carbon buildup or degraded rubber components, so a compression test is mandatory before purchase.

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: A proper reconditioned OM611 engine is the sweet spot for most buyers. A reputable rebuild will address the common failure points by upgrading or replacing the swirl flap system, fitting new injector seals, and refreshing the timing chain and guides, giving the engine a fresh lease on life.

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: A full OM611 engine rebuild is justified for high-mileage Sprinter commercial vans or classic W210/W211 E-Class restorations where originality and maximum longevity are required. An upgraded rebuild should include line-boring the block, new pistons/rings, and a balanced crankshaft.

buyingGuide.supplyFitLine: Sourcing and fitting through our vetted network ensures your OM611 engine is installed by specialists familiar with early Mercedes CDI systems, backed by a nationwide warranty.
buyingGuide.vehicleValueNote: Because the OM611 is typically found in W203, W210, W211, and early Sprinter vehicles valued between £1,500 and £6,000, a full replacement can represent a significant portion of the host's worth. If the lowest viable replacement cost exceeds approximately 60% of the vehicle's current market value, evaluate scrap value before committing .

items.answer: A reconditioned Mercedes OM611 engine typically costs between £2,500 and £4,200 for supply only . Fitted costs generally range from £3,300 to £5,100 depending on the specialist, while used units can be found from £1,200 but carry higher risk due to the engine's age and mileage. → Compare OM611 engine replacement quotes today

items.question: What is the most common failure on the OM611 engine?
items.answer: The most documented issues are swirl flap actuator failure, injector seal weeping ("Black Death"), and timing chain guide wear at high mileage. Swirl flap motor failure triggers limp mode and is a routine fix, whereas injector seal failure causes black carbon buildup and rough idling but is a cheap and preventative maintenance item. → Get quotes for a rebuilt OM611 with these issues resolved

items.question: Which Mercedes models use the OM611 engine?
items.answer: The OM611 was fitted to the W203 C-Class (C 200 CDI, C 220 CDI), the W210 and W211 E-Class (E 200 CDI, E 220 CDI), and the first-generation Sprinter vans (208 CDI, 211 CDI, 213 CDI, 216 CDI), serving as Mercedes' pioneering CDI diesel. → Check your registration to confirm your exact OM611 fitment

items.question: Should I buy a used or reconditioned OM611 engine?
items.answer: A reconditioned OM611 is strongly recommended over a used unit. A proper rebuild will proactively address the common failure points by upgrading or replacing the swirl flap system, fitting new injector seals, and refreshing the timing chain and guides, whereas used engines often hide stretched chains and carboned manifolds. → Compare reconditioned OM611 engine prices from UK specialists

items.question: What is the difference between OM611.940, .950, and .960?
items.answer: The OM611.940 is the 2.1L entry-level variant, the OM611.950 is the 2.2L naturally aspirated version with a longer stroke for higher low-end torque in heavier cars, and the OM611.960 is the 2.2L turbocharged variant requiring a higher-capacity mechanical injection pump and upgraded cooling for commercial van applications. → Enter your reg above to identify your exact OM611 sub-code ═══════════════════════════════════════
